# Challenges with Missing Data {#sec-intro}

In most statistical and machine learning literature, datasets are assumed to be complete. For instance, in case of tabular data, it is assumed that all features are observed for each sample. Similarly, in the case of multivariate time-series data, it is often assumed that all features for each sample are measured at the same time points. In practice however, datasets are often *incomplete*, with some features unobserved for certain samples, or *fragmented* in case of time-series data, with observations or features missing at different timepoints across samples.

A similar issue is label missignesss, which has given rise to the field of semi-supervised learning. Label missingness refers to the scenario where only some samples in the dataset are labelled. However, approaches to semi-supervised learning often assume similar distribution of the missing labels as the available labels, which is often not reflected in real world scenarios. An example for this is the task of anomaly detection, where often only some positive samples are labelled, and the unlablled part of the dataset consists overwhelmingly of non-anomalous samples.

In this chapter, I will introduce the different types of missingness that has been proposed in the literature, as well as propose a new classification of missingness based on a different perspective. I will also discuss how the semi-supervised setting can be viewed as a special case of missing data, and how it can be incorporated into the overall missingness framework.

## Motivation for dealing with missingness

### Missing data in the real-world setting and Challenges - Missing attributes <!-- mention 'privacy issues' in the conclusion of thesis instead of the introduction-->

A common scenario in which this type of missingness is encountered is biomedical data and electronic health records. Patients usually have different lengths of stay in a hospital, and are prescribed different medical tests depending on their symptoms. Consolidating this data into a singular structure usually results in extensive missingness across features and timepoints, resulting in a incomplete, fragmented and sparse data structure. For example, in @boneDensityData the collected dataset records bone density of children across ages. Although in aggregate the dataset covers age-ranges from 9 to 26 years old, each individual only has 2-4 measurements, typically measured over not more than 5 years.

### Mathematical formulation

Throughout this thesis, I will use the standardised notation encouraged by most machine learning conferences. Italicized letters will indicate deterministic quatities. Normal small letters indicate numbers ($x,y,t$), bold small letters indicate vectors ($\vx,\vy,\vt$), bold capital letters indicate matrices ($\mX,\mY,\mT$), capital letters in sans-serif fonts indicate tensors $(\tX,\tY,\tT)$ and blackboard bold capital letters indicate sets ($\sX,\sY,\sT$) (with the exception of $\E$ and $\P$ which are defined below). The non-italicized versions of these indicate random quatities; random variables are $\rx,\ry,\rt$, random vectors are $\rvx,\rvy,\rvt$ and random matrices are $\rmX,\rmY,\rmT$. Elements of higher order arrays like vectors, matrices, and higher order tensors are denoted by regular versions of the bold letters with subscripts: $\evx_1,\emX_{11},\etX_{111},\ervx_1,\ermX_{11}$, etc. For a matrix $\mX$, $\mX_{i,:}$ and $\mX_{:,i}$ will denote the $i^{th}$ row and column respectively.

When two random variables $\rx$ and $\ry$ are independent, I will denote that as $\rx\independent\ry$.

I will denote the vectorization of a matrix $\mX$, which means stacking the columns of the matrix sequentially, as
$$\vec(\mX)=[\mX_{:,1}^\trans\quad\mX_{:,2}^\trans\quad\cdots\quad\mX_{:,n}^\trans]^\trans$$
The determinant of a matrix $\mA$ will be denoted by $|\mA|$, and Kronecker product of two matrices $\mA_{m\times n}$ and $\mB_{p\times q}$ is an $mp\times nq$ matrix defined as
$$
\mA\kron\mB\deff\begin{bmatrix}
\emA_{11}\mB &\emA_{12}\mB&\cdots\emA_{1n}\mB\\
\emA_{21}\mB &\emA_{22}\mB&\cdots\emA_{2n}\mB\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\emA_{m1}\mB &\emA_{m2}\mB&\cdots\emA_{mn}\mB\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
The generalized psedo-inverse [@pseudoinverse, pp. 20] of a matrix $\mA$ will be denoted by $\mA^-$, which simply indicates that $\mA\mA^-\mA=\mA$. It should be clear that the choice of $\mA^-$ is not unique for a singular matrix $\mA$, *i.e.* if $|\mA|=0$. In cases where a unique choice is necessary, I will use the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse [@penrosePseudoinverse] $\mA^+$, which is defined by the following properties:
$$\mA\mA^+\mA=\mA\qquad\mA^+\mA\mA^+=\mA^+\qquad(\mA\mA^+)^*=\mA\mA^+\qquad(\mA^+\mA)^*=\mA^+\mA$$.

I will denote the probability of an event $E$ as $\P(E)$, expectation of a random variable $\rx$ as $\E[\rx]$, its variance as $\Var(\rx)$, and its covariance with another random variable $\ry$ as $\Cov(\rx,\ry)$. I will denote the variance-covariance matrix of a random vector $\rvx$ as $\Var(\rvx)$. For a matrix $\mSigma$, $\norm{\rvx}_\mSigma$ will denote the Mahalanobis norm [@mahalanobisDistance] of $\rvx$ with covariance $\mSigma$, defined as $\norm{\rvx}_\mSigma\deff\rvx^\trans\mSigma^-\rvx$.

I will also denote the KL divergence of 2 distributions $P$ and $Q$ over the support $\sX$ as
$$\KL(P||Q)\deff\int_{x\in\sX}P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}dx$$
The Cartesian product of two sets $\sA$ and $\sB$ will be denoted by $\sA\times\sB$.

## Problem Formulation (Add more discussion about the definitions, to motivate to non-experts)

I will adopt notation similar to @hyperimpute for the problem formulation and denote missing values as `NaN`. Let $\rvx\in \sX=(\sX_1\times\ldots\sX_D)$ be a D-dimensional random vector. The entries of this random vector can be continuous ($\sX_d=\R$) or categorical ($\sX_d=\{1,\ldots,K_d\}$) random variables, for $d\in\{1,\ldots,D\}$. We do not have complete observational access to $\rvx$; instead our observation is mediated by a random masking vector $\rvm\in\{0,1\}^D$. If $\ervm_d=1$, then $\ervx_d$ is observed. Assume that $\rvm$ follows a distribution $\pmask$, and the data $\rvx$ follows a distribution $\pdata$. <!--Say there are $N$ samples, and index everything by $i$, where $i$ is the index of the sample-->

## Types of missingness

Classical literature mainly distinguishes three main missingness mechanisms depending on the relationship between the probability of missingness with the observed and unobserved data [@typesOfMissingness]. These can be distinguished based on the form and properties of $\pmask$.

### \acr{MCAR}

\acr{MCAR} is a missingness mechanism where the probability of missingness is independent of the observed and unobserved data. In other words, the missingness is completely random and does not depend on any of the observed or unobserved data. This is equivalent to the statement that $\rvx\independent\rvm$. This also indicates that each component of $\vm, m_i$, is an independent Bernoulli random variable with probability $p_i$ independent of $\vx$.

::: {exm-MCAR}
## Missing Completely at Random

:::

### \acr{MAR}

The missigness mechanism \acr{MAR} indicates that the probability of missingness depends only on the observed values. In more techinicality, let $\rvx$ and $\rvm$ be partitoned as $\{\rvx_1,\rvx_2\}$ and $\{\rvm_1,\rvm_2\}$ respectively, such that $\rvx_1$ is always observed, that is, $\rvm_1=\mathbf{1}$. Then, $\rvx$ is said to be \acr{MAR} if $\pmask$ depends only on $\rvx_1$. A simple model of this, and one I will use to demonstrate and evaluate imputation methods on the \acr{MAR} scenario, is
$$
\pmask(\rvm_2\mid\rvx_1)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-\rmW\rvx_1)},
$${#eq-MAR}
where $\rmW$ is a random matrix.


### \acr{MNAR}

If data is missing by the \acr{MNAR} mechanism, the probability of missingness depends both on the observed and the unobserved data. Mathematically, $\pmask$ depends on all elements of $\rvx$. A model similar to @eq-MAR can be developed for this scenario, but a much simpler model that still allows us to evaluate methods and derive theoretical guarantees is Gaussian self-masking
$$
\pmask(\ervm_i\mid\ervx_i) = K_i\exp(-\frac{(\ervx_i-\tilde{\mu}_i)^2}{2\tilde{\sigma}_i^2})
$$
where $\tilde{\mu}_i$ and $\tilde{\sigma}_i^2$ are the mean and variance of the observed values of the $i^\text{th}$ components of $\rvx$, and $0<K_i\leq 1$ is a scaling factor.

::: {#rem-gaussianSelfMasking}
## Gaussian Self-Masking
This model encodes dependence only on the (possibly) missing value. However, dependence on the observed values is covered under the \acr{MAR} scenario, so I chose to model the \acr{MNAR} scenario by only explicitly encoding dependence on the missing values.
<!--(Explain this more, say "I chose this because the other case is covered in MNAR")-->
:::
